# 2 Kings Chapter 8 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 228v–229v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_008_page_001.jpg, 2KI_008_page_002.jpg, 2KI_008_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Now Elisha had warned the woman whose son he had brought back to life, "Take your family and move away — go wherever you can — because the LORD has decreed a famine that will strike this land for seven years."

**2** So the woman did as the man of God said. She took her family and lived in Philistine territory for seven years.

**3** When the seven years were over, she came back from Philistia and went to the king to appeal for the return of her house and her land.

**4** At that very moment, the king happened to be talking with Gehazi, Elisha's servant. "Tell me about all the remarkable things Elisha has done," the king was saying.

**5** And just as Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had brought a dead boy back to life, the boy's mother walked in to make her appeal! "My lord the king," Gehazi said, "this is the woman — and this is the son Elisha brought back to life!"

**6** The king questioned the woman, and she confirmed everything. He then assigned an official to her case, ordering, "Give her back everything that belonged to her, including all the income the land has produced from the day she left until now."

**7** Elisha traveled to Damascus. Ben-hadad king of Aram was ill, and when someone told him, "The man of God is here,"

**8** the king told Hazael, "Take a gift and go meet the man of God. Ask him to inquire of the LORD whether I will recover from this illness."

**9** So Hazael went to meet Elisha, bringing an enormous gift — forty camel-loads of the finest goods Damascus had to offer. He stood before Elisha and said, "Your son Ben-hadad, king of Aram, has sent me to ask: 'Will I recover from this illness?'"

**10** Elisha told him, "Go and tell him, 'You will certainly recover.' But the LORD has shown me that he will in fact die."

**11** Then Elisha stared at Hazael with a fixed, unblinking gaze — held it so long that Hazael looked away in shame. And the man of God began to weep.

**12** "Why is my lord weeping?" Hazael asked. Elisha answered, "Because I know the terrible things you are going to do to the people of Israel. You will set their fortified cities ablaze, slaughter their young men, smash their children against the ground, and rip open their pregnant women."

**13** "But I'm nobody!" Hazael protested. "How could a mere dog do something so monstrous?" Elisha replied, "The LORD has shown me that you will become king of Aram."

**14** Hazael left Elisha and returned to his master. "What did Elisha say?" Ben-hadad asked. "He told me you will certainly recover," Hazael replied.

**15** But the next day, Hazael took a thick cloth, soaked it in water, and pressed it over the king's face until he suffocated. Then Hazael became king in his place.

**16** In the fifth year of King Joram of Israel — while Jehoshaphat was still king of Judah — Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat became king of Judah.

**17** He was thirty-two when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for eight years.

**18** He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, just as Ahab's family had done — because he had married Ahab's daughter. He did what was evil in the LORD's sight.

**19** But the LORD refused to destroy Judah, for the sake of his servant David, since he had promised to keep a lamp burning for David's descendants forever.

**20** During Jehoram's reign, Edom broke free from Judah's control and crowned their own king.

**21** Joram crossed over to Zair with all his chariots and attacked by night, breaking through the Edomites who had surrounded him and the chariot commanders. But his troops fled back to their homes.

**22** So Edom has been independent from Judah to this day. Libnah also revolted at that time.

**23** The rest of what Jehoram did is recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

**24** Jehoram died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Ahaziah succeeded him as king.

**25** In the twelfth year of King Joram of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah.

**26** Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for one year. His mother was Athaliah, a granddaughter of King Omri of Israel.

**27** He followed the ways of Ahab's family and did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just like the house of Ahab — for he had married into Ahab's family.

**28** He went with Joram son of Ahab to fight King Hazael of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and the Arameans wounded Joram in battle.

**29** King Joram returned to Jezreel to recover from his wounds. And Ahaziah king of Judah went down to Jezreel to visit him while he was recovering.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — "The LORD has decreed a famine":** The Hebrew says YHWH "called" the famine — summoned it like a servant. This is the woman from chapters 4-5 (the Shunammite), returning to bookend Elisha's miracle ministry with a practical survival story. God restores her dead son in chapter 4; now he protects her livelihood through advance warning.

**Verses 4-5 — The cosmic coincidence:** The timing is extraordinary. The king happens to be asking Gehazi about Elisha's miracles — specifically the raising of the dead boy — at the exact moment the boy's mother walks in. The narrator presents this as divine orchestration without saying so explicitly. Providence works through "coincidence."

**Verse 11 — Elisha weeps:** This is one of the most emotionally raw moments in the Elisha cycle. The prophet stares at Hazael until the man can't meet his gaze, and then breaks down crying. He isn't weeping for Hazael — he's weeping for the future victims. Prophetic knowledge is a burden: Elisha sees the massacres before they happen and can do nothing to prevent them.

**Verse 13 — "How could a mere dog?":** Hazael's protest is either genuine horror or calculated deflection. Either way, it's chilling — the man who says "I could never do such things" becomes the man who does them. Power transforms. The passage is a study in how ordinary people become perpetrators of extraordinary evil.

**Verse 19 — The Davidic lamp:** Despite Jehoram's alliance with Ahab's family and his evil reign, YHWH preserves Judah for David's sake. The "lamp" (*nir*) is a metaphor for dynastic continuity. This single verse carries the weight of the entire Davidic covenant theology — grace for the many because of the promise to one.

*— PNEUMA*
